label: Polyhedra As Checkable Surfaces
notes: Open with the central shift from a solid object to a surface with ledgers. The lecture treats a polyhedron through local angle sums, global counts, cut choices, and gluing certificates. Emphasize that the same object will be read as geometry, topology, and a graph at different moments.

label: Three Ledgers For One Object
notes: Frame the chapter as three mutually correcting ledgers. Incidence counts keep track of topology, angle sums keep track of curvature, and cut or gluing graphs keep track of how a surface can be flattened or assembled. Students should expect every visual claim to have a numerical certificate beside it.

label: Regular Vertex Inequality
notes: Use the regular vertex inequality as the first example of local geometry controlling a global classification. If q regular p-gons meet at a convex vertex, the total angle must be less than a full turn. This single strict inequality leaves only a small finite menu.

label: The Five Regular Convex Solids
notes: Read the table as a consequence of the previous inequality, not as a memorized list. The defect column is the amount of curvature placed at each vertex. Small positive defects allow the surface to close; zero would be flat tiling behavior rather than a convex corner.

label: Euler Characteristic
notes: Move from local angle arithmetic to global incidence arithmetic. For convex polyhedra the boundary has the topology of a sphere, so vertices minus edges plus faces equals two. The point is not the number alone but the fact that many different decompositions preserve it.

label: Genus Changes The Ledger
notes: Contrast the sphere ledger with surfaces that have handles. The orientable formula two minus twice the genus is a reminder that Euler characteristic is topological data, while convex polyhedra live in the genus zero row. This slide prevents students from overextending V minus E plus F equals two.

label: Curvature Lives At Vertices
notes: Introduce polyhedral curvature as concentrated at vertices. Each face is flat and each edge can be unfolded locally, so the only place curvature remains is the angular gap at a vertex. The diagram asks students to see curvature as missing angle rather than as smooth bending.

label: Polyhedral Gauss-Bonnet
notes: State the executable version of Gauss-Bonnet for a convex sphere-like polyhedron. Add the vertex defects and the total is four pi, regardless of whether the surface is a tetrahedron, cube, or icosahedron. The global invariant is recovered by a finite sum.

label: Rigidity Is A Different Question
notes: Separate incidence and curvature checks from rigidity. Cauchy rigidity says a convex polyhedron with matching corresponding faces cannot flex into a noncongruent convex polyhedron. The proof idea follows sign changes around a cycle, so the visual focuses on a graph certificate rather than a 3D animation.

label: Flexibility And Volume
notes: Give students room for the important contrast: nonconvex polyhedra can be flexible even though convex ones are rigid under Cauchy's hypotheses. Bellows-type results add that volume can remain fixed during a flex. The lesson is that face congruence, rigidity, convexity, and volume are distinct statements.

label: Cut Trees And Unfoldings
notes: Turn to planar developments. A cut set that opens a polyhedron without disconnecting the faces corresponds to a spanning tree in the dual graph. For a cube this means five dual edges are chosen, but the spanning-tree condition alone does not guarantee a nonoverlapping net.

label: Cube Net As Dual Choice
notes: Read the cube net and the dual tree together. The planar cross is one possible development, while the small graph records which face adjacencies were not cut. This is a useful computational habit: the drawing is geometric, but the certificate is graph-theoretic.

label: Shortest Paths Become Straight
notes: Explain why unfolding is useful for geodesics. When a shortest path crosses a sequence of faces, unfolding those faces into one plane turns the path into a straight segment. The apparent 3D problem becomes a planar straightness test after the right cuts are made.

label: Cut Loci And Source Unfolding
notes: Describe the cut locus as the branching set that prevents a global one-piece flattening from a source point. Cutting along that locus gives a source unfolding where shortest paths from the source are represented by straight radial segments. The emphasis is organization, not a full algorithmic proof.

label: Alexandrov Gluing Ledger
notes: Reverse the logic: instead of cutting a polyhedron into polygons, glue polygons and ask whether they form a convex polyhedron. The ledger conditions are metric edge matching, angle totals at most two pi at glued vertices, and total positive curvature four pi. These are existence conditions, not construction steps.

label: What To Carry Forward
notes: Close by returning to the chapter's recurring habit. Polyhedra become manageable when each geometric picture is paired with the right finite certificate: angle defects, Euler characteristic, sign cycles, dual spanning trees, straight unfolded paths, and gluing ledgers.
